verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r4 cards (6 true, 6 false; the balance holds) against their man7.org pages. Every URL returned 200. Pinned versions from each page's COLOPHON: execve(2), inode(7), chown(2), capabilities(7), credentials(7) and passwd(5) come from man-pages 6.19; sudoers(5) from Sudo 1.9.18 (upstream Git, 2026-05-23); su(1) from a util-linux 2.43 development snapshot from Git; usermod(8) and newgrp(1) from shadow-utils 4.19.0.

Cards that pass, with the deciding quote:
- sr4-02: execve(2) says "Linux (like most other modern UNIX systems) ignores the set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits on scripts."
- sr4-03: execve(2) says the effective-ID change is not performed if "the underlying filesystem is mounted nosuid". Its NOTES say kernels either refuse execution with EPERM or ignore the bits, which matches the explanation; "depending on kernel behavior" would read better as "depending on the kernel version".
- sr4-04: inode(7) says "files created there inherit their group ID from the directory, not from the effective group ID of the creating process".
- sr4-06: chown(2) says "When the owner or group of an executable file is changed by an unprivileged user, the S_ISUID and S_ISGID mode bits are cleared ... since Linux 2.2.13, root is treated like other users." The section list does not name this fact explicitly, but it is a special-bit behaviour operators run into, so I judged it in scope.
- sr4-07: capabilities(7) says "Linux divides the privileges traditionally associated with superuser into distinct units, known as capabilities". It is rated difficulty 3 but reads as medium at most.
- sr4-08: sudoers(5) says "it validates the invoking user's credentials, not the target user's (or root's) credentials. This can be changed via the rootpw, targetpw and runaspw flags", and targetpw "is off by default". One residual risk: some distributions have shipped an /etc/sudoers containing "Defaults targetpw" (historically openSUSE). Read as "the default file a distribution installs", the phrase "default sudoers policy" could be argued the other way. Rewording it to "With sudoers' built-in defaults" would close that gap. sudo-rs (Ubuntu) also asks for the invoking user's password, so the card is not distribution-bound.
- sr4-09: su(1) under --login says "change to the target user's home directory".
- sr4-11: usermod(8) says "If the user is currently a member of a group which is not listed, the user will be removed from the group. This behaviour can be changed via the -a option, which appends the user to the current supplementary group list."
- sr4-12: the answer is correct. credentials(7) supports it only by inference: "A child process created by fork(2) inherits copies of its parent's user and groups IDs. During an execve(2), a process's real user and group ID and supplementary group IDs are preserved", and setgroups(2) is the call that modifies the list. No allowed page states outright that editing /etc/group leaves running shells unchanged; initgroups(3) and newgrp(1) do not say it either. I did not flag it, because no better official URL exists. The explanation would be stronger if it named the remedy, for example: "New membership applies at the next login, or in a new shell started with newgrp."

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 12 r5 cards (6 true, 6 false; average statement length 86.3 for true and 86.7 for false; all statements are 120 characters or fewer and all explanations 240 or fewer). - 02: execve(2) NOTES: "there is no new process; many attributes of the calling process remain unchanged (in particular, its PID)". A non-leader thread calling execve takes over the leader's PID, but the PID itself stays the same, so the answer holds.

verdicts.notes:
All 12 source URLs (github.com/systemd/systemd/blob/v262/man/*.xml) return 200 and are official v262 man sources, which the prompt allows. I read the raw XML of each page and checked every card against it.

The 9 cards that pass, with the sentence that settles each:
- 02 (timer has no ExecStart=): "For each timer file, a matching unit file must exist, describing the unit to activate when the timer elapses."
- 03 (/etc over /usr/lib): "Unit files found in directories listed earlier override files with the same name", and /etc/systemd/system comes before /usr/lib in the system load-path table.
- 04 (systemctl edit makes a drop-in): "If --full is specified, a replacement for the main unit file will be created or edited. Otherwise, a drop-in file will be created or edited." The default name is override.conf.
- 06 (enable does not start): "Note that this does not have the effect of also starting any of the units being enabled."
- 07 (mask blocks dependency activation): mask "prohibits all kinds of activation of the unit, including enablement and manual activation."
- 08 (SIGTERM then SIGKILL): KillSignal= "Defaults to SIGTERM" and is "usually followed by SIGKILL".
- 09 (Restart=on-failure ignores SIGTERM): systemd.service treats SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGTERM and SIGPIPE as clean "except for Type=oneshot", and on-failure excludes those four signals. Type=simple is therefore the right scope.
- 10 (journalctl -u): adds _SYSTEMD_UNIT matches "along with additional matches for messages from systemd and messages about coredumps".
- 12 (Storage=volatile): "If volatile, journal log data will be stored only in memory, i.e. below the /run/log/journal hierarchy".

Balance is 6 true and 6 false. Average length is 97.5 for true statements and 98.5 for false ones. With all three proposed replacements it would be about 104 against 99.8, still within the 5-character rule. No r12 fact is duplicated in another section: r6 tests SIGKILL as uncatchable, and r5 tests systemd as PID 1.

Minor points that do not need a flag:
- 12 is close to a definition card ("volatile" suggests non-persistent), but the section lists it explicitly and a learner could plausibly answer true.
- 10 is easy, but it is in scope.
- 11's explanation leaves out the --directory exception, which is harmless at this depth.
- No card covers socket or mount units, is-active/is-enabled, -p/-k/--since, or the removal of SysV scripts in 260. That is a coverage gap, not a defect.

duplicates.why: Both cards rest on the rule that single quotes around $HOME stop it from expanding. sr7-08 uses a single-quoted here-doc delimiter (<<'EOF') with literal $HOME, and sr8-04 single-quotes '$HOME' as an argument. A learner who knows one can answer the other by analogy, so they are opposite-answer twins in practice. Dropping sr8-04 removes the overlap; it is close to a strawman ('can expand' inside single quotes is something few who studied would believe). The alternative is to keep sr8-04 for r8 and rewrite sr7-08 with a double-quoted or backslash-quoted delimiter ("EOF" or \EOF), which tests the here-doc rule in its own right.

chown(2) states these two as one distinction: only a privileged process may change a file's owner, while the owner may change the group to one of their own groups. The prompt says the two sides of one distinction are one fact. sr3-08 (an owner giving the file away with chown is False) is the classic trap. sr3-09 (an owner using chgrp to pick one of their own groups is True) is the other side, and it is easier to guess.

conflictGroups.name: stderr-fd-two
conflictGroups.why: The sr7-03 statement ('command 2>&1 > log sends standard error into log') treats fd 2 as standard error, which is the answer to sr7-02 (whether 2> selects standard output: False).

conflictGroups.name: single-quote-literal
conflictGroups.why: sr7-08 (True) shows single quoting keeping $HOME literal, which gives away sr8-04 (single-quoted $HOME expands: False). This is also listed as a duplicate.

conflictGroups.name: shell-does-globbing
conflictGroups.why: sr8-09 says Bash passes an unmatched *.log on as a literal argument. sr8-08 says 'Bash's default * expansion', and its explanation mentions 'Bash's default filename-expansion settings'. Both tell the player that the shell, not ls, expands patterns, which answers sr8-07 (False).

conflictGroups.name: nohup-vs-ampersand
conflictGroups.why: The sr6-06 explanation says that with a plain nohup command 'the shell still waits for the command to finish', so a separate operator is needed for background running. That points straight at sr6-07 (& lets the shell continue: True). sr6-07 in turn hints that backgrounding is &'s job, not nohup's.

conflictGroups.name: stopped-job-resume
conflictGroups.why: sr6-08 (bg %1 can resume a stopped job: True) shows that a stopped job needs an explicit resume command. That answers sr5-06 (a stopped process resumes when CPU time becomes available: False). The sr5-06 explanation ('needs a continuation signal') in turn supports sr6-08.

conflictGroups.name: foreground-process-group
conflictGroups.why: The sr5-11 explanation ('Terminal input normally belongs to the foreground process group') and the sr6-08 explanation ('remains outside the terminal's foreground process group') both point to the terminal-to-foreground-group link that sr6-03 tests (Ctrl-C sends SIGINT to the foreground process group). sr6-08 also hints at sr5-11's background-read behaviour.

conflictGroups.name: nice-direction
conflictGroups.why: The sr5-08 explanation says a higher nice value means lower priority. With that, sr5-09 (an unprivileged user may raise the nice value of their own process) becomes an easy True, since giving up priority is harmless. In the other direction, sr5-09 shows that ordinary users may raise nice values, which hints that raising them is not a privilege grab.

conflictGroups.name: boot-lifetime-storage
conflictGroups.why: The sr1-07 explanation says /run holds runtime data cleared at boot. The sr1-06 explanation says /var/tmp files survive reboots, so /var is the persistent side. Together they answer sr12-12 (Storage=volatile keeps journals under /var/log/journal: False; the answer is /run/log/journal).

conflictGroups.name: usr-holds-programs
conflictGroups.why: The sr1-03 statement ('/bin holds separate copies of the executables in /usr/bin') and its explanation tell the player that /usr holds installed executables, which answers sr1-04 (/usr as the parent of home directories: False).

conflictGroups.name: rename-open-descriptor
conflictGroups.why: sr10-12 explains that tail -F follows the name and reopens it after rotation, which implies that an open descriptor keeps pointing at the renamed file. That is the fact sr2-11 tests (True).

conflictGroups.name: symlink-stored-text
conflictGroups.why: The sr2-09 explanation ('retaining a relative target as relative text') shows that a symlink stores only the literal target text, with no record of the creator's working directory. That hints at sr2-07 (relative target resolved from the creation working directory: False).

conflictGroups.name: directory-search-bit
conflictGroups.why: The sr3-03 explanation ('needs write and search permission on the containing directory') calls the directory permission 'search', which points to x, not r. That hints at sr3-02 (the read bit grants traversal: False).

conflictGroups.name: unlink-directory-control
conflictGroups.why: The sr4-05 explanation describes the sticky bit as adding 'deletion and renaming restrictions' to a directory. This shows that deletion is controlled at the directory level, which answers sr3-03 (a file's own write bit authorizes removing its name: False).

conflictGroups.name: owner-may-change
conflictGroups.why: Three statements share the template 'a file's owner can <change attribute>', with answers F (chown), T (chgrp) and T (chmod), so seeing them together invites guessing by contrast. The sr4-06 explanation ('including changes performed by root') also hints that ownership changes are root's job, which helps answer sr3-08.

conflictGroups.name: setuid-exceptions
conflictGroups.why: sr4-01 (True) carefully says 'setuid ELF executable', which signals that interpreter scripts (sr4-02) and other cases behave differently. The sr4-02 and sr4-03 explanations ('Linux ignores the set-user-ID bit on interpreter scripts', 'confer no privilege') frame both as exceptions to the sr4-01 rule. A player can read the general rule and its exceptions off one another.

conflictGroups.name: sigterm-sigkill-escalation
conflictGroups.why: sr12-08 (systemd sends SIGTERM first and uses SIGKILL on a service that fails to stop) presents SIGTERM as the polite default and SIGKILL as the unstoppable fallback. That hints at sr6-01 (kill's default is SIGTERM) and at sr6-02 (a process can catch SIGKILL to clean up: False).

conflictGroups.name: subshell-vs-current-shell
conflictGroups.why: The sr7-11 explanation (a cd inside $() runs in a subshell and leaves the outer shell unchanged) and the sr8-02 explanation (source runs in the current shell context) state the same contrast from opposite sides, so each card supports the other's answer.

conflictGroups.name: redirect-truncation
conflictGroups.why: The sr7-06 statement says 'With Bash noclobber off'. sr7-12 explains that noclobber protects existing files from > and that >| overrides it. sr7-01 says >> preserves the existing content. Together they tell the player that plain > truncates the target, which answers sr7-06 (sort data > data preserves contents: False).

conflictGroups.name: host-key-change
conflictGroups.why: The sr11-05 explanation says known_hosts exists to detect 'an unexpected key change', which hints that no checking mode quietly accepts a changed key. That answers sr11-06 (accept-new accepts a changed key: False).

conflictGroups.name: unit-override-location
conflictGroups.why: sr12-03 (True: /etc/systemd/system wins over /usr/lib/systemd/system, 'letting local configuration override the packaged definition') shows that local overrides live outside the vendor file. That hints at sr12-04 (systemctl edit opens the vendor unit file by default: False).

conflictGroups.name: install-links
conflictGroups.why: The sr12-07 explanation ('Disabling removes installation links but leaves other activation routes available') shows that enable and disable only manage [Install] links. That hints at sr12-06 (enable brings the service into the running state: False).

conflictGroups.name: terminal-control-keys
conflictGroups.why: These are a near-mirrored true/false pair on one template, 'With normal settings, the terminal driver sends/uses <signal> ... on Ctrl-<key>': Ctrl-C/SIGINT is True and Ctrl-Z/SIGSTOP is False. Dealt together, they invite contrast guessing between SIGSTOP and SIGTSTP.

conflictGroups.why: Both are b3 false cards on one template: a counting option 'counts X as separate/another <unit>' (grep -c and wc -l). Seeing one makes the other easy to spot as the same distractor.

All 144 cards read (b1 48, b2 48, b3 48). Each section has 6 true and 6 false cards. All 144 ids and factKeys are unique. Within each section, the average length of true and false statements is within 5 characters (largest gap: r8, where true statements are 4.3 characters longer; r4, where false are 3.3 longer). Hedge 'can' is balanced across the deck (20 true, 20 false), and so is 'by default/default' (8 true, 8 false). The exploitable tells are in narrower wording and in templates.

WORD TELLS (statement text):
1. 'even when / even if / including' marks True 7 of 8 times. True: sr1-07, sr2-05, sr3-11, sr3-12, sr8-05, sr9-01, sr12-07. False: sr10-08 only. This is the strongest wording tell: a statement that adds a reassuring scope clause is almost always true.
2. FHS verb tell in r1. Every 'FHS places ... under /x' statement is True (sr1-02, sr1-05, sr1-11, 3 of 3). Every FHS statement with another verb ('uses', 'treats', 'assigns') is False (sr1-04, sr1-06, sr1-08, 3 of 3). A player can answer all six FHS cards from the verb alone.
3. A tool-possessive subject ("Bash's", "GNU tar's", "OpenSSH's", "GNU chmod's") marks False 5 of 6: sr7-03, sr8-07, sr8-08, sr11-02, sr11-07 are False, and only sr3-06 is True.
4. 'retain / preserve / keep' leans True, 7 of 10. True: sr3-04, sr4-11, sr5-05, sr6-08, sr8-05, sr10-03, sr10-12. False: sr5-12, sr7-06, sr12-12.
5. 'treats/counts/stores X as <noun>' leans False, 6 of 8. False: sr1-06, sr1-10, sr9-03, sr10-10, sr10-11, sr11-11. True: sr8-06, sr8-09.
6. 'the caller' leans True, 4 of 5. True: sr2-05, sr4-01, sr6-01, sr10-05. False: sr12-11.
7. Minimiser words mark False 2 of 2 ('alone' in sr2-12, 'simply because' in sr5-06). 'direct/directly' marks False 2 of 2 (sr4-02, sr12-04). 'automatically' marks False 2 of 3 (sr4-12 and sr6-06 False, sr4-04 True).
8. 'In Bash,' leans slightly True within b2: 9 true, 6 false.

RECURRING FALSE TEMPLATES (the prompt allows at most two false statements per template):
A. Reversal of a direction or order, 8 false cards: sr2-08 (ln operand order), sr5-08 (nice direction), sr8-03 (PATH first vs last), sr8-12 (&& runs on failure), sr10-04 (parent before children with -delete), sr10-07 (LC_ALL=C gives the user's collation), sr11-07 (-L listener on the remote side), sr12-11 (-b with no offset gives the previous boot). A player who flips 'first/last/higher/remote/previous' claims to False will often be right.
B. Sibling swap, where an option or item is given the job of its nearest neighbour, 7 false cards: sr1-08 (/ for /root), sr4-08 (target vs invoking user's password), sr6-04 (SIGSTOP for SIGTSTP), sr7-02 (stdout for stderr), sr9-10 ($NF as NF), sr11-02 (-J as gzip instead of xz), sr11-04 (private key for public key).
C. '<X> can <break a documented restriction>', 11 false cards: sr2-04, sr3-01, sr3-07, sr3-08, sr4-02, sr4-03, sr5-02, sr6-02, sr7-11, sr8-04, sr11-06. The word 'can' is balanced, but in these false cards it always claims an override of a well-known prohibition, while true 'can' cards describe ordinary capabilities.
D. 'X counts Y as another/separate unit', 2 cards, both in b3: sr9-03, sr10-11. 'X keeps/preserves ... until Z', 2 cards: sr5-12, sr7-06. Each is at the limit of two.
E. Parallel-template pairs with opposite answers, which invite contrast guessing: sr6-03/sr6-04 ('With normal settings, the terminal driver ... on Ctrl-'), and sr3-08/sr3-09/sr3-12 ('A file's owner can ...').

B3 (GPT-6.1 Sol) VERSUS B1/B2 (GPT-6 Pro) WORDING HABITS:
1. Subject prefix. In b3, 23 of 48 statements open with 'GNU' and 13 open with 'GNU `cmd`'. In b1 the counts are 4 and 1; in b2 they are 2 and 2. b3 never uses 'Linux' as a subject, while b1 and b2 use it 22 times. b2's equivalent habit is the 'In Bash,' opener (15 times). These prefixes are balanced by answer, so they are style differences rather than tells, but b3 reads visibly different.
2. Precondition guards on true statements. b3 true cards often carry lawyer-like scoping clauses: sr9-04 'when that symlink appears as a command-line operand', sr9-05 'After a successful scan with zero matching lines', sr9-09 'With default input settings', sr9-12 'In a normal multi-file run', sr10-05 'when the caller supplies input but omits a command name', sr10-09 'from input lines that contain a colon', sr12-03 'For matching system unit filenames', sr12-08 'With default kill settings ... that fails to stop'. b3 false cards rarely carry such guards; where they have a leading clause, it only names the option under test (sr12-09, sr12-11, sr12-12). Within b3, leading condition clauses split 9 true to 6 false, and trailing guards split about 8 true to 2 false. A practised player can read 'heavily hedged precondition' as True.
3. Longer statements. Mean length is 92.7 characters for true and 91.7 for false in b3, against 83 to 89 in b1 and b2. The maximum is 116 in b3 against 106 in b1 and b2. r12 is the longest section (about 98 on average).
4. Explanation style. b3 explanations are shorter on average (113 characters, against 126 in b1 and 137 in b2). Only 21 of 48 have two sentences, against 35 in b1 and 45 in b2. 19 of 48 begin with a lowercase flag or command ('-J selects xz', 'tr maps', 'grep -c counts', 'accept-new adds', 'journalctl -b selects'); b1 has none and b2 has 5. b3 joins clauses with semicolons more often (5, against 2 and 1). b3 almost never uses the b1/b2 habit 'rather than' (1, against 11 and 7). Some b3 explanations are terse to the point of not standing alone (sr9-02, sr11-02, sr11-06).
5. 'default' density. b3 uses 'default/by default' in 10 statements (6 true, 4 false), against 1 in b1 and 5 in b2, so the word's frequency jumps across the batch boundary.
6. b3 false statements favour the 'counts/treats X as <unit>' frame (sr9-03, sr10-10, sr10-11, sr11-11). b1 and b2 false statements favour '<X> can <override a prohibition>' (template C, 10 of its 11 cards come from b1 and b2).

rewrite.reason: weak_card that had to be rewritten: dropping sr1-02, sr1-09 and sr1-11 would leave r1 at 3 true and 6 false. This uses the verifier's replacement, shortened to one fact. Confirmed in FHS 3.0 section 3.7: "No binaries may be located under /etc" and "it must be static and cannot be an executable binary".
rewrite.statement: FHS forbids placing executable binaries under the `/etc` configuration hierarchy.
rewrite.explanation: FHS 3.0 limits /etc to static, local files that control how programs operate, and states that no binaries may be located under it.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: path_resolution(7) does not settle precedence when the owner is also in the group. acl(5) does. Its ACCESS CHECK ALGORITHM says that if the effective UID matches the owner, access is granted only if ACL_USER_OBJ contains the requested permissions, else denied. Its CORRESPONDENCE section says the owner permissions correspond to ACL_USER_OBJ. The statement now uses the verifier's clearer wording, which drops the clumsy 'can combine' and keeps False.
rewrite.statement: When a file's owner is also in its group, Linux grants the owner the union of the owner and group permission bits.
rewrite.explanation: Linux checks the owner class first: for the file's owner, only the owner permission bits decide access, even when the group bits would grant more.
rewrite.misconception: Owner and group permission bits combine when the owner belongs to the file's group.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: path_resolution(7) does not support the read-means-list half. The GNU coreutils Mode-Structure node supports both halves: "For directories, this means permission to list the contents of the directory" for read, and "permission to access files in the directory" for execute. gnu.org refused connections, so I read it through the Web Archive. The statement is unchanged and the explanation is aligned to the page.
rewrite.statement: A directory's read bit grants permission to traverse that directory during pathname lookup.
rewrite.explanation: For a directory, the execute bit grants access to the files inside it during lookup, while the read bit lets a user list the names it contains.
rewrite.misconception: Directory read permission also provides search permission.
rewrite.sourceTitle: GNU Coreutils manual: Structure of File Mode Bits

rewrite.reason: source_problem: bash(1) never mentions the execute bit. The Bash manual's Shell Scripts node says Bash "reads and executes commands from the file" given as the first argument, and that a script "may be made executable" with chmod for running it through PATH (read through the Web Archive). The statement is reworded with the same fact and answer, which removes the true-card hedge 'can' and the 'even when' tell.
rewrite.statement: `bash script.sh` runs the commands in a readable script whose mode is 0644.
rewrite.explanation: Given as an argument, the file is opened and read by Bash, so read permission is enough. The execute bit matters when the script itself is run as a command, for example found through PATH.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: pidfd_open(2) only implies PID reuse. pidfd_send_signal(2) states it: "the originally intended target process has terminated and its PID has been recycled for another process". The explanation now matches that page; the statement is unchanged.
rewrite.statement: Linux keeps a terminated process's PID reserved until the next system boot.
rewrite.explanation: Once a process has terminated, Linux can recycle its PID for another process, so a stored PID may later refer to an unrelated process.
rewrite.misconception: Process IDs remain reserved for the entire boot, even after the processes disappear.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: bash(1) does not state the search order. environ(7) PATH does: it is used by sh(1) and other programs, and "The list of prefixes is searched from beginning to end ... until a file with execute permission is found." The statement is unchanged and the explanation is aligned.
rewrite.statement: When Bash searches PATH for an executable, it chooses the last matching directory's executable.
rewrite.explanation: PATH is searched from beginning to end, and the first directory holding a matching file with execute permission wins, so earlier entries take precedence.
rewrite.misconception: Later PATH entries take precedence over earlier matching entries during a search.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'leaving the boot offset unspecified' is also true of `-b <previous boot ID>`. The rewrite names a bare -b. journalctl.xml v262 says "The argument may be empty, in which case logs for the current boot will be shown" and "-1 the boot before last". I wrote 'bare' instead of the verifier's 'with no boot ID or offset' to avoid a negation.
rewrite.statement: Running a bare `journalctl -b` shows the log messages recorded during the previous boot.
rewrite.explanation: With an empty argument, journalctl -b shows the current boot. An offset such as journalctl -b -1 selects the boot before it.
rewrite.misconception: Omitting journalctl's boot argument selects the previous boot.

In r1 all three flagged cards were true, so dropping all of them would have left r1 at 3 true and 6 false. sr1-02 was therefore rewritten with the verifier's replacement, the FHS "no binaries under /etc" rule, confirmed on FHS 3.0 section 3.7.

cards.statement: FHS forbids placing executable binaries under the `/etc` configuration hierarchy.
cards.explanation: FHS 3.0 limits /etc to static, local files that control how programs operate, and states that no binaries may be located under it.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. FHS 3.0 section 3.7 says "No binaries may be located under /etc", and its footnote limits 'executable binary' to machine code, so scripts in /etc are not a counterexample.

cards.statement: Linux grants a file owner who is also in the file's group the union of the owner and group bits.
cards.explanation: Linux checks the owner class first: for the file's owner, only the owner permission bits decide access, even when the group bits would grant more.
cards.reason: Applied the wording lens's shorter statement (96 instead of 114 chars). It keeps the same fact and answer. With it, r3 averages 85.3 for true and 87.5 for false, inside the 5-char rule. Checked acl(5) ACCESS CHECK ALGORITHM step 1: when the effective UID matches the owner, ACL_USER_OBJ alone grants or denies access.

cards.statement: A directory's read bit grants permission to traverse that directory during pathname lookup.
cards.explanation: For a directory, the execute bit grants access to the files inside it during lookup, while the read bit lets a user list the names it contains.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The coreutils Mode-Structure node says read on a directory means listing its contents and execute means access to the files in it.

cards.statement: `bash script.sh` runs the commands in a readable script whose mode is 0644.
cards.explanation: Given as an argument, the file is opened and read by Bash, so read permission is enough. The execute bit matters when the script itself is run as a command, for example found through PATH.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The Bash manual's Shell Scripts node says Bash reads and executes commands from a file given as its argument, and ties the execute bit to the PATH case.

cards.statement: Linux keeps a terminated process's PID reserved until the next system boot.
cards.explanation: Once a terminated process has been removed from the kernel process table, Linux can recycle its PID for another process, so a stored PID may later name an unrelated one.
cards.reason: Fact lens fix. 'Once a process has terminated' was wrong for zombies: wait(2) NOTES says a zombie keeps its PID and its process-table slot until a wait removes it. I phrased the fix as removal from the process table rather than 'reaped by its parent's wait'. That stays exact (orphaned zombies are reaped by init or a subreaper) and does not give away sr5-05, which tests whether the zombie keeps its status for the parent. pidfd_send_signal(2) confirms that PIDs are recycled.

cards.statement: When Bash searches PATH for an executable, it chooses the last matching directory's executable.
cards.explanation: PATH is searched from beginning to end, and the first directory holding a matching file with execute permission wins, so earlier entries take precedence.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. environ(7) PATH says the list is searched from beginning to end until a file with execute permission is found.

cards.statement: Running a bare `journalctl -b` shows the log messages recorded during the previous boot.
cards.explanation: With an empty argument, journalctl -b shows the current boot. An offset such as journalctl -b -1 selects the boot before it.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. journalctl.xml v262 says an empty argument shows the current boot and that -1 is the boot before last.

cards.statement: GNU `grep -F 'a.b' file` treats the dot in the pattern as an ordinary character to match.
cards.explanation: With -F, GNU grep interprets the supplied pattern literally, including punctuation with special regex meanings.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. grep(1) says -F interprets PATTERNS as fixed strings, not regular expressions.

cards.statement: On Linux, the link() call returns an error when a root process asks it to hard-link a directory.
cards.explanation: Linux forbids directory hard links through link(). Administrative privilege does not provide an exception to that restriction.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. link(2) lists 'EPERM oldpath is a directory' with no privilege condition, unlike the protected_hardlinks EPERM case.

cards.statement: For an unprivileged process, permission to chmod a file depends on owning it rather than on its write bit.
cards.explanation: chmod(2) requires the caller's effective UID to match the file's owner, unless the caller is privileged, so an owner can change the mode of a read-only file.
cards.reason: Applied the wording lens fix. A process with CAP_FOWNER can chmod files it does not own, so the statement now names the unprivileged caller. Confirmed on chmod(2): "The effective UID of the calling process must match the owner of the file, or the process must be privileged (Linux: it must have the CAP_FOWNER capability)." The statement is 106 chars, and r3 averages stay within 5 chars (85.3 true, 87.5 false).
